Consult Summary:
- 45-year-old female marathon trainee with 2-week history of right knee pain and audible clicking during activity, most consistent with patellofemoral/overuse knee pathology (runner's knee).

History:
- Presenting complaint and timeline:
  - Right knee pain with clicking for ~2 weeks, worsened after increasing running mileage over the past month.
  - Pain typically begins ~20 minutes into a run (~2.5–3 miles); has required stopping on recent runs.
  - Initial mild swelling after first long run that improved with ice; currently no persistent swelling at rest.
  - One transient episode of right toe tingling after a run (resolved).
- Associated symptoms / systems review:
  - No locking, no giving-way/instability, full ability to straighten and fully flex the knee.
  - No persistent calf pain, no redness, no fever, no systemic symptoms.
  - No problems with stairs or normal walking.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No ongoing swelling or warmth now; no persistent numbness; no colour/temperature change of leg; no other joints affected.
- Past medical history, allergies, medications:
  - Past: LASIK; prior ER visit for presumed kidney stone / severe UTI. Prior ice-hockey fall months ago with a large bruise (no documented fracture/repair).
  - Medications: Vitamin D, melatonin, occasional ibuprofen (~400 mg), occasional naproxen (Aleve), occasional alprazolam (Xanax). Uses cannabis occasionally. No medication allergies reported in the consult.
- Social / preventive health:
  - Active runner training for a marathon; plays ice hockey. Lives in London. No family history of rheumatologic disease documented.

Examination:
- Vitals: none recorded.
- Observations from video/telephone assessment:
  - Patient reports full range of motion (can fully flex and extend).
  - No current visible swelling or warmth of the knee on video; no locking observed.
  - Pain localized to the central knee with some shift to the right side on patient report; clicking reported with flexion/extension (noted during gym/ab exercises and running).
  - Able to walk and use stairs without difficulty during the consult.

Impression:
- Working diagnosis:
  1. Patellofemoral pain syndrome / patellar maltracking (high likelihood)
     - Rationale: Classic overuse history (recent mileage increase), anterior/central knee pain that begins after a set duration of running (~20 minutes), activity-provoked pain, transient swelling after exertion, and clicking with flexion/extension.
  2. Iliotibial band (ITB) syndrome or lateral tendinopathy (moderate likelihood)
     - Rationale: Timing of pain onset during runs and patient report of pain moving to the right lateral area are compatible with ITB friction syndrome.
  3. Meniscal or intra-articular cartilage injury (moderate likelihood)
     - Rationale: Intermittent clicking and prior knee trauma (ice-hockey fall) could reflect a meniscal or chondral lesion; less likely currently because there is no locking or persistent mechanical block.
- Other considerations (lower likelihood but noted in DDx): reactive bursitis / patellar tendinopathy, DVT (low likelihood given absent calf pain/warmth and localized mechanical symptoms), early OA, transient nerve compression explaining one-off toe tingling.

Plan:
- Immediate management (as advised and agreed in consult):
  - Continue ice therapy for symptomatic relief.
  - Reduce running intensity/mileage; avoid running through pain. Modify training while symptomatic.
  - Prescribe a stronger oral anti-inflammatory (clinician to send prescription to pharmacy); counsel to take with food and not to combine with other NSAIDs (do not take simultaneously with ibuprofen).
- Next steps / referrals:
  - Referral to physiotherapy for detailed assessment and individualized rehabilitation (biomechanics, strengthening, gait/running form, patellar tracking management).
  - Offer in-clinic assessment if physiotherapy wait is long or symptoms warrant earlier review.
  - Consider imaging (e.g., MRI of knee) if symptoms persist despite conservative management or if physio/clinical exam suggests intra-articular pathology (meniscal/cartilage lesion).
- Safety net / red flags:
  - Seek urgent assessment if knee develops persistent swelling, increasing heat/redness, systemic symptoms/fever, or if the knee locks and cannot be bent/straightened.
- Follow-up:
  - Review after physiotherapy appointment or earlier if symptoms worsen or new concerning signs develop. (Clinician indicated referral and prescription will be sent.)

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - No documented medication allergy list (patient did not state any).
  - No formal vitals (BP, HR, temperature).
  - No objective in-person physical exam findings (limited by video consult).
  - No exact NSAID prescribed name/dose recorded in the transcript (clinician stated they would send a stronger anti-inflammatory).
  - No imaging or baseline labs available.
  - No tobacco use status beyond occasional cannabis; no DVT risk-factor checklist documented (e.g., prior thrombosis, OCP use).
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - None required to note; DDx reasoning is consistent with the transcript. (DDx includes DVT as a low-likelihood consideration; transcript provides no supporting signs.)
- Transcript quality:
  - Adequate for history-taking; patient communication clear. Limitations: no formal vitals or hands-on physical exam recorded; assessment constrained by video—objective signs (point tenderness, ROM with clinician exam, swelling measurement) are absent.
